claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature plastic strain than commercially used pure tungsten.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature toughness than commercially used pure tungsten.
Equimolar mixing of W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr produces random atomic-scale lattice distortions.
The atomic-scale lattice distortions enhance dislocation pinning.
The atomic-scale lattice distortions promote dynamic recovery during deformation.
The equimolar combination of W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr provides solid-solution strengthening.
The alloy's random atomic field impedes dislocation motion.
High-temperature deformation activates dynamic recovery in WTaTiVZr.
Dislocation pinning and dynamic recovery jointly delay plastic failure.
Dislocation pinning and dynamic recovery jointly increase toughness.
Relative to pure tungsten, WTaTiVZr will exhibit higher plastic strain before failure at 800–1200°C under otherwise matched loading conditions.
Relative to pure tungsten, WTaTiVZr will absorb more energy during deformation at 800–1200°C under otherwise matched loading conditions.
Deformed WTaTiVZr will show greater dislocation accumulation than deformed pure tungsten.
Deformed WTaTiVZr will show microstructural signs of dynamic recovery.
Matched high-temperature tensile and creep tests with in-situ TEM can distinguish the proposed behavior of WTaTiVZr from that of pure tungsten.
A temperature-series study can help separate the contributions of dislocation pinning and thermally activated dynamic recovery.
The proposed mechanism is limited to equimolar WTaTiVZr versus pure tungsten at 800–1200°C and similar strain rates.
Failure of WTaTiVZr to show significantly higher plastic strain and toughness than pure tungsten under the controlled tests would falsify the hypothesis.
